items.prompt_md: In the two-heap running-median design, which heap holds the smaller half, and what kind of heap is it?
options: A min-heap holding the smaller half
A max-heap holding the smaller half, so its top is the largest of the small values
A max-heap holding the larger half
A single sorted list split in the middle
items.answer: A max-heap holding the smaller half, so its top is the largest of the small values
items.explanation_md: The median lives at the border, so the lower half must expose its **largest** element (max-heap) and the upper half its **smallest** (min-heap). A min-heap for the lower half would expose its minimum, which is nowhere near the middle.

items.prompt_md: Python's `heapq` is a min-heap only. How do you build the max-heap for the lower half?
options: Call `heapq.heapify(reverse=True)`
Sort the list descending before every push
Store negated values and negate again when reading
Use `heapq.heappush_max`, which flips the order
items.answer: Store negated values and negate again when reading
items.explanation_md: Pushing `-x` makes the smallest stored value correspond to the largest real value. `heapify` has no `reverse` flag, and re-sorting on every push would destroy the O(log n) bound.

items.prompt_md: Which pair of invariants must hold after every insertion?
options: Both heaps are full to the same capacity, and both are sorted
Every element of `low` is at most every element of `high`, and the sizes differ by at most one
`low` and `high` contain the same multiset of values
The top of `low` equals the top of `high`
items.answer: Every element of `low` is at most every element of `high`, and the sizes differ by at most one
items.explanation_md: Ordering says the halves do not overlap; balance says the border is at the middle. Lose either and the tops no longer identify the median.

items.prompt_md: What is the time complexity of one `add_num` and one `find_median` in the two-heap design?
options: O(n) and O(1)
O(log n) and O(log n)
O(log n) and O(1)
O(1) and O(1)
items.answer: O(log n) and O(1)
items.explanation_md: Adding does a constant number of pushes and pops, each O(log n). The median only peeks at one or two heap tops, which is O(1). O(1) for add is impossible because each push sifts.

items.prompt_md: After `n` insertions, how much memory does the two-heap structure use?
options: O(log n), since heaps are balanced trees
O(n), each value is stored once across the two heaps
O(1), only the two tops are kept
O(n^2) because each add touches both heaps
items.answer: O(n), each value is stored once across the two heaps
items.explanation_md: To keep answering medians you must remember every value: each one is in exactly one heap. Only the tops are read, but the rest must still be stored, or later rebalancing would have nothing to move.

items.prompt_md: A solution stores the numbers in a plain list and calls `sorted(...)` before every `find_median`. With `n` adds each followed by a median query, what is the total time?
options: O(n log n)
O(n^2 log n)
O(n)
items.answer: O(n^2 log n)
items.explanation_md: Each query sorts up to `n` items at O(n log n), and there are `n` queries, giving O(n^2 log n). The heaps do the same job in O(n log n) total.

items.prompt_md: `low` has 3 elements and `high` has 3 elements. Where does the median come from?
options: The top of `low` alone
The top of `high` alone
The average of the top of `low` and the top of `high`
The sum of both tops
items.answer: The average of the top of `low` and the top of `high`
items.explanation_md: An even count has two middle values: the largest of the lower half and the smallest of the upper half. Their average is the median. With an odd count the extra element sits in `low`, so its top alone is the answer.

items.prompt_md: In `add_num`, the new value is pushed to `low`, then low's maximum is popped and pushed to `high`. Why do it in this order?
options: It guarantees everything left in `low` is at most everything in `high`, whichever side the new value belongs on
It makes `heappush` run in O(1)
It avoids having to negate values
It keeps `low` sorted in descending order
items.answer: It guarantees everything left in `low` is at most everything in `high`, whichever side the new value belongs on
items.explanation_md: If the new value is big, it is the max of `low` and crosses over immediately. If it is small, the old max crosses instead. Either way the ordering invariant holds with no explicit comparison. Heaps are never fully sorted, and the push cost is unchanged.

items.prompt_md: A developer pushes raw (non-negated) values into the heap used as `low` and reads `low[0]` as the lower half's maximum. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; `heapq` automatically keeps the largest value on top
`low[0]` is the smallest value of the lower half, so the median is computed from the wrong element
It raises an exception on the second push
Only duplicates are mishandled
items.answer: `low[0]` is the smallest value of the lower half, so the median is computed from the wrong element
items.explanation_md: `heapq` always keeps the minimum on top. Without negation the border element is not accessible in O(1), and the ordering invariant silently breaks.

items.prompt_md: The stream's values are all integers between 0 and 100. What simpler structure also supports a fast running median?
options: A count array of 101 buckets scanned to find the middle rank
A segment tree over the insertion order
A linked list sorted by arrival time
Nothing simpler exists; two heaps are required
items.answer: A count array of 101 buckets scanned to find the middle rank
items.explanation_md: With a tiny fixed range, bucket counts give a median in O(101), effectively O(1) per query, with no heaps at all. Interviewers like hearing that the data range can change the best design.

items.prompt_md: Why can't a single min-heap of size `k` answer "what is the median so far" the way it answers "what is the k-th largest so far"?
options: Heaps cannot store more than `k` items
The median's rank changes as the count grows, so no fixed size `k` keeps the middle on top
A min-heap cannot hold negative numbers
The median is always the minimum, so a heap is unnecessary
items.answer: The median's rank changes as the count grows, so no fixed size `k` keeps the middle on top
items.explanation_md: The k-th largest has a fixed rank, so a size-`k` heap pins it to the top. The median is the n/2-th rank and moves, which is why the structure needs two heaps that rebalance.

items.prompt_md: A sensor feed sends one reading at a time. After each reading, a dashboard must show the middle value of everything received so far. Which technique fits?
options: Sort the whole history after every reading
A hash map of reading counts
Two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half
Binary search over the reading values
items.answer: Two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half
items.explanation_md: A growing collection with a middle-rank query after every insert is the two-heap setup: O(log n) insert, O(1) query. Sorting per reading is far slower, and counts or binary search do not track a moving middle.

items.prompt_md: You are given a fixed array and one query: report its median once. Which is the most reasonable approach?
options: Two heaps, inserting all the elements
Sort the array and read the middle (or use quickselect for average O(n))
A sliding window of size two
A trie of the digits
items.answer: Sort the array and read the middle (or use quickselect for average O(n))
items.explanation_md: With a static array and one query there is nothing to maintain incrementally, so sorting (or selection) is simplest. Two heaps pay off only when queries interleave with insertions. The other two options do not relate to ranks.

items.prompt_md: A game server keeps a leaderboard stream and must always expose the score of the player currently ranked exactly 10th from the top. Scores only get added. Which technique fits best?
options: Two heaps balanced around the median
A size-10 min-heap whose top is the 10th largest
A monotonic stack
Prefix sums
items.answer: A size-10 min-heap whose top is the 10th largest
items.explanation_md: The rank is fixed (10th largest), so one bounded min-heap is enough, and its top is the answer. Two heaps are for a rank that moves with the size, like the median.

items.prompt_md: Customer orders arrive in real time. After each order you must report the median order value, and you may see millions of orders. Which technique fits?
options: Dynamic programming over order sequences
A union-find over order ids
Two heaps splitting values into a lower half and an upper half
Keep a running total and divide by the count
items.answer: Two heaps splitting values into a lower half and an upper half
items.explanation_md: A running total gives the mean, not the median, which depends on order statistics. Two heaps keep the border between halves available in O(1) with O(log n) updates.

items.prompt_md: Given a list of daily temperatures, for each day find how many days until a warmer one. Which technique fits?
options: Two heaps around the median
A max-heap of all temperatures
A monotonic stack of indices
Binary search on the answer
items.answer: A monotonic stack of indices
items.explanation_md: This is a next-greater-element question: a stack of waiting days resolves each when a warmer day arrives. There is no median or running rank here.

items.prompt_md: You need the sum of the best contiguous block of exactly 5 readings in an array, scanning left to right once. Which technique fits?
options: A fixed-size sliding window with a running sum
Two heaps
A trie
Topological sort
items.answer: A fixed-size sliding window with a running sum
items.explanation_md: The windows are contiguous and fixed-length, so adding the entering value and removing the leaving one is O(1) per step. Heaps add log factors and are not needed since no order statistic is asked for.

items.prompt_md: Many meetings with start and end times are given. Find the minimum number of rooms so no meetings overlap in a room. Which technique fits?
options: Two heaps around the median
A min-heap of end times while sweeping meetings sorted by start
A sliding window of size two
Prefix sums of durations
items.answer: A min-heap of end times while sweeping meetings sorted by start
items.explanation_md: The question is how many meetings are active at once; a min-heap of end times frees rooms as meetings finish. It is still heap-family, but a single heap, not a two-heap median structure.

items.prompt_md: A sorted array is given and you must find the first position where the value is at least a given number, fast. Which technique fits?
options: Two heaps
Hash map lookup
Binary search on the sorted array
A min-heap of all elements
items.answer: Binary search on the sorted array
items.explanation_md: Sorted input plus a threshold query is binary search in O(log n). Building heaps would throw away the sorted order you already have.

items.prompt_md: Given an array and a target, find the number of pairs of different indices whose values add to the target, in one pass over an unsorted array. Which technique fits?
options: A hash map of counts for complement lookup
Two heaps
A segment of the array via a sliding window
A max-heap of pair sums
items.answer: A hash map of counts for complement lookup
items.explanation_md: Pairing by target is membership lookup: store counts of values seen, check for the complement. No median or rank question appears, so heaps are the wrong tool.

items.prompt_md: A trading app receives prices one by one and must keep the lower 50 percent and upper 50 percent of prices separated so that the boundary price is always instantly available. Which technique fits?
options: A monotonic queue
Prefix sums
Union-find
A max-heap for the lower half paired with a min-heap for the upper half
items.answer: A max-heap for the lower half paired with a min-heap for the upper half
items.explanation_md: Keeping two halves split at the middle, with the boundary on top of each heap, is exactly the two-heap structure. The other options track neither ranks nor a changing border.
